definition: Usurp means to seize power or a position without the right to it.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word usurp. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know usurp should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: While the guildmaster lay fevered, his son-in-law usurped the chair at council, sealing letters with a ring nobody had given him.
To meddle is to poke into business that isn't yours; meddle stops far short of usurp — the meddler interferes, the usurper takes the chair.
To encroach is gradual — a fence creeping a foot a year into a neighbor's field; encroach stops short of usurp, which seizes the whole office in one stroke.

Seize is the all-purpose grab — police seize contraband, armies seize bridges, banks seize collateral, by force or by law. Usurp is narrower and always illegitimate: it takes an office, title, or right that lawfully belongs to someone else. Anything can be seized; only another's rightful place is usurped.

To hijack is to take something over mid-course, by force and in the moment — a plane, a meeting, a conversation. Usurp works quieter and aims higher: with paperwork and nerve it takes the office or the authority itself, not just the controls for an afternoon.

The reed warbler builds one of the neatest nests on the river, and the common cuckoo builds none at all.
Instead, the cuckoo waits for a warbler pair to finish their work, slips in while they forage, and leaves a single egg among their clutch.
Naturalists of the last century wrote that the hatchling usurps the nest, and the verb is precise: within hours the young cuckoo heaves the warblers' own eggs over the rim, one by one.
What it takes is not merely food or shelter but the whole rightful place of the brood that should have been — the warblers feed the intruder as though it were their own.
The pair labor on for weeks, raising a chick three times their size, tenants in service to the occupier of their own home.
